sections.label: Overview
sections.content: This section gives a clear introduction to the project or subject. It sets the context, explaining what the work is about and why it exists. A good overview helps the reader understand the purpose without going into too much detail. It should briefly cover the idea, the approach, and the outcome you’re aiming for. Think of it as the first impression that prepares someone for everything that follows.

sections.label: Work Details
sections.content: This is where you break down what actually went into the work. It can include the process, tools used, decisions made, and challenges faced along the way. Instead of being too technical, keep it structured and easy to follow. Highlight the steps that mattered the most and explain why certain choices were made. This section helps others understand not just what you did, but how you did it.

sections.label: Outcome
sections.content: Here you present the final result and what came out of the work. It could be the finished product, key learnings, or the impact it created. This section should connect back to the overview and show whether the original goal was achieved. You can also mention what you would improve or do differently next time, giving it a more complete and thoughtful ending.

sections.label: THE PROBLEM
sections.content:
Planning a trip to Pondicherry, I searched for recommendations and hit a wall — every result was a bloated blog post with too much noise and not enough signal. I wanted a simple list of places with a Google Maps link. That gap was the product idea.

Digging deeper, I spotted a second problem: the internet was flooding with generic, AI-generated travel content. Trust was eroding. Travelers wanted human experiences, not algorithm output.

sections.label: Positioning & Differentiation
sections.content:
I positioned the product as a community-curated directory — the opposite of AI-generated content. To back this up with real data, I ran a 2-week community research exercise on Reddit across 5–6 cities, collecting genuine local recommendations. This wasn't just market research — it became the product's core differentiator.

Key positioning choice: "Community-curated" wasn't a tagline — it was a trust signal the audience immediately connected with. Early users didn't just approve; they started contributing unprompted, reducing my data-collection load organically.

sections.label: Go-to-Market: One Channel, Full Focus
sections.content:
With a full-time job, I had limited bandwidth. I made a deliberate GTM call: pick one channel and go deep on it. I chose Reddit — where the audience already was, asking for travel recommendations. I engaged genuinely on existing posts across all the cities on my site. What started as a daily activity scaled down to 2–3 sessions a week as the channel matured.

Result: 60–80 users a day from 30 minutes of weekly effort. 2,000 users in the last 30 days — entirely from one channel, zero paid spend.

sections.label: Product Evolution
sections.content:
The MVP was a minimal directory — city pages with place listings and Google Maps links. After launch, I identified two gaps: it felt sparse, and it didn't offer enough value to retain users. I iterated deliberately.

What I added: A city dashboard (daily budget, transport, best time to visit, recommended stay) to improve stickiness. Download and share list features for brand distribution. A map view for discoverability. I tracked usage on each and kept features that showed signal — even low usage — over vanity features that added nothing.

sections.label: Validation & Feedback Loop
sections.content: I built a feedback popup directly into the site to close the loop with users. 154 submissions collected. 152 positive, 2 negative. I treated this as the clearest signal that the core value proposition was working — and used it to stay focused on what was already resonating rather than chasing scope creep.

sections.label: Monetization Thinking
sections.content: I approached monetization with the same intentionality as the product itself. Google Ads would have been the obvious route — but it conflicted with the clean, trust-first experience I'd built. I ruled it out. Instead, I went with affiliate marketing, integrating it as a native product category within each city page rather than an intrusive popup. The experience stays seamless; the brand integrity stays intact.

sections.label: SEO & Long-term Growth
sections.content: Organic search was the long game. I started SEO activities from day one, knowing results would compound slowly. From near-zero impressions in January to ~30 per day in April, the curve is moving. Direct traffic is also climbing — a potential early signal of Google-driven discovery as authority builds.
